title: Google Calendar
seoTitle: Design a Calendar Service Like Google Calendar
description: Design Google Calendar — creating events and recurring events, inviting attendees, free/busy lookups, time zones, and reminders.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.text: Understanding the Problem

blocks.title: What is Google Calendar?
blocks.text: Google Calendar lets people schedule events, invite others, see when colleagues are free, and get reminders before events start.
Functional Requirements
Core Requirements

items: Users should be able to create, edit and delete events, including recurring events.
Users should be able to invite attendees, who can accept or decline.
Users should be able to view their calendar for a day, week or month.
Users should receive reminders before events.

blocks.text: Below the line (out of scope):

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

blocks.text: Non-Functional Requirements
Core Requirements

items: Strong consistency for a user's own edits (read-your-writes); invitee calendars can update within seconds.
Reminders must fire on time, reliably, for hundreds of millions of users.
Correct handling of time zones and daylight-saving changes.

The Set Up
Defining the Core Entities

items: **Event**: title, start/end (with time zone), organizer, recurrence rule (RRULE), location.
**Attendee**: an invite linking a user to an event, with response status.
**Event exception**: a modified or cancelled single occurrence of a recurring series.
**Reminder**: when to notify a user about an event.

blocks.text: API or System Interface
High-Level Design
1) Users should be able to create events, including recurring ones

The **Event Service** stores each event once. A recurring event stores its **recurrence rule** (RFC 5545 RRULE) rather than one row per occurrence — "every Monday forever" can't be materialised. Edits to a single occurrence are stored as **exceptions**.
2) Users should be able to invite attendees
Creating an event writes an Attendee row for each invitee. Invitations are delivered asynchronously (email + push) via a queue, and each attendee's response updates their row.
3) Users should be able to view their calendar

The **Calendar View Service** fetches the user's events that overlap the requested range (their own plus those they're invited to), expands recurring events into concrete occurrences for that window, applies exceptions, and converts times into the viewer's time zone.
4) Users should receive reminders

Each reminder is scheduled as a job at `start - offset`. A scheduler (like the one in [Job Scheduler](/learn/system-design/problem-breakdowns/job-scheduler)) fires it and hands it to the notification system.
Potential Deep Dives
1) How do we store and query recurring events efficiently?

approach.text: Write a row for every instance of a recurring event.

challenges.text: Infinite series can't be stored; editing "all future events" means rewriting thousands of rows.

blocks.title: Store the rule, expand at read time

approach.text: Store the RRULE plus exceptions, and expand only within the requested window when rendering.

challenges.text: To find events overlapping a range, you must know the series' overall span; store a computed `seriesEnd` (or null for infinite) so queries can filter quickly.

approach.text: Keep the rule as the source of truth, but materialise occurrences for a rolling window (e.g. the next 6 months) into an index table used for fast range and free/busy queries. Re-materialise when the series changes.

challenges.text: Two representations to keep in sync, but range queries become simple index scans.

blocks.text: 2) How do we handle time zones correctly?

Store event times as **local time plus an IANA time zone** (e.g. `09:00 America/New_York`), not just UTC. A weekly 9am meeting must stay at 9am local time across daylight-saving changes; storing UTC alone would shift it by an hour twice a year. Convert to the viewer's zone only when rendering.
"All-day" events have no time zone — a birthday on March 3 is March 3 everywhere. Treat them as dates, not timestamps.
3) How do we answer "when is everyone free?"

Free/busy lookups read each attendee's materialised occurrences for the window from the index, merge their busy intervals, and return the gaps. Cache per-user busy intervals for short periods; they're read far more often than they change.
Final Design

quiz.question: Why store a recurrence rule instead of every occurrence?
options: Series can be infinite and edits would rewrite many rows
quiz.explanation: Rules plus exceptions represent any series compactly.

quiz.question: How should a weekly 9am meeting be stored to survive DST changes?
options: As local time plus an IANA time zone
As a Unix timestamp per week
quiz.explanation: Local time + zone keeps the meeting at 9am local year-round.

quiz.question: How is a change to one occurrence of a recurring event stored?
options: As an exception linked to the series
quiz.explanation: Exceptions override or cancel individual occurrences.

quiz.question: What makes free/busy lookups fast?
options: Expanding rules on every request for every attendee
A materialised occurrence index for a rolling window
quiz.explanation: Precomputed occurrences turn free/busy into range scans.
